title: Why ROI spreadsheets don't sell software: create obvious value and price to budgets
summary: Jason Cohen explains why ROI and cost-savings arguments never closed a sale at Smart Bear, even when the math was sound and customers asked for it. Savings are unmeasurable and budgets are siloed, so he advises building value so obvious it needs no calculation and pricing by willingness to pay and budget structure.

principles.text: ROI and cost-savings arguments don't close sales, even when the math is sound and the customer asks for it.
principles.quote: But this argument never worked, not once, even though the reasoning is sound and customers requested it. The reason is that these "savings" aren't how budgets actually work.

principles.text: Productivity gains are real but unmeasured in practice, so the savings you promise are invisible to the buyer.
principles.quote: But it's also essentially impossible to measure, and is in fact not measured. So the "savings" are invisible, even if real.

principles.text: Budgets are siloed: savings in one budget (salaries) never fund spend in another (tools), so "it pays for itself" fails.
principles.quote: Never once in my seven years selling software at Smart Bear, whether 10 seats or 2500 seats, did a company make a decision in which savings in the "Salaries" budget resulted in an increase to the "Tools" budget.

principles.text: Customers buy on belief that the product helps, not on a spreadsheet; they either believe or they don't.
principles.quote: Spreadsheets are worthless--they either believe, or they don't.

principles.text: Create so much value that no computation is needed: change workflows so drastically that customers can't live without it.
principles.quote: create so much value that there's no need to "compute" it.

principles.text: Price by ability and willingness to pay and by business model structure, matching the buyer's budget constraints, not as a direct function of "value".
principles.quote: price according to ability and willingness to pay and the structure of your business model, rather than as a direct function of so-called "value."
